headline: A judge threw out the DOJ's Alaska suit.
summary: Alaska votes Tuesday with two Dan Sullivans on its Senate ballot. The Justice Department sued to have the second Dan's votes set aside and studied, and the result held, if the senator lost. On Sunday Judge Sharon Gleason threw it out: no "workable plan" that kept ballots secret, and days too late. The DOJ says it will appeal.

cover_question.q: Why can't they check the votes?

cover_answer: Ballots are secret. The DOJ had no plan that kept them so.
table_question: Should anyone get to see how you voted, even to check for cheating?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Alaska, two men named Dan Sullivan want the same job, and both names are on the voting paper. The president's lawyers asked a judge to pull out one Dan's votes and check them, like scooping marbles out of a jar before the count. On Sunday the judge said no. Votes are secret. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Marbles out of a jar is a thing they can see, and "votes are secret" is a rule they can keep. Who sued whom can wait.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them a jar of marbles and one rule: votes are secret, nobody peeks. The lawsuit and the appeal stay out, because this age can't yet hold the abstract part and doesn't need to. Expect "so who wins?" Nobody yet. Alaska votes Tuesday.

8-12.script: Alaska votes Tuesday with two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. The Justice Department sued to set the second Dan's votes aside if the senator lost. On Sunday Judge Sharon Gleason threw it out: ballots are secret, and the DOJ had no plan to keep them so. Like a referee refusing a new rule after kickoff.
8-12.why: Sue, judge, no, with the reason attached. A referee who won't change the rules mid-game is a call this age makes at recess.
8-12.why_long: This age is testing whether adults apply rules evenly, and the script hands them the chain whole: a lawsuit, a judge, a no, with the reason attached. Secret ballots are a rule they can check, and a referee who won't change the rules after kickoff is a call they make at recess. Expect "so did the DOJ lose?" Say yes, for now.

13-17.script: Should a court set aside ballots to check what voters meant? The DOJ asked in Alaska, and Judge Sharon Gleason said no: "no workable plan" that kept ballots secret, and days too late. Second: the DOJ says she never ruled on whether the second Dan is a decoy. Does that soften the loss?
13-17.why: A real quote on each side. Let them weigh procedure against substance first.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a judge refused the DOJ's plan because it could not keep ballots secret, and the DOJ says she never ruled on whether the second Dan is a decoy. The script hands them both. Expect "was he planted?" Say the judge didn't decide that, and nobody has proved it.

5-7.a: Nobody knows yet. Alaska votes Tuesday, and the judge said no pulling any votes out first.

8-12.q: Why can't they check the votes?
8-12.a: Ballots are secret. The DOJ had no plan to study them and keep that.
No. The DOJ says it will appeal. And the vote is Tuesday.

13-17.q: Did the judge say the second Dan is real?
13-17.a: No. She said the DOJ had no workable plan and no power over Alaska.

13-17.q: Why does two days out matter?
13-17.a: Many Alaskans already voted. The judge said it came too late.
